title: Immunology & Infectious Disease
description: Innate and adaptive immunity, complement and inflammation, antibodies and their classes, B and T cells, MHC, vaccines, hypersensitivities, epidemiology terms, and classic pathogens with their diseases.

cards.title: Which complement proteins assemble into the membrane attack complex that punches pores in target cell membranes?
cards.body:
C5b, C6, C7, C8 and several C9 (C5b–C9)

C5b binds C6, C7 and C8, and the complex then polymerizes many **C9** molecules into a ring-shaped pore. Water and ions rush in, and the cell lyses.

Key idea: all three complement pathways (classical, lectin and alternative) end at this same lytic complex.
Example: people who lack C5–C8 are prone to recurrent $\textit{Neisseria}$ infections.
cards.searchQuery: membrane attack complex C5b-C9 complement pore lysis

cards.title: Which enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus breaks the $\beta$-1,4 bond between NAG and NAM in peptidoglycan?
cards.body:
Lysozyme.

It weakens the cell wall and causes osmotic lysis. It works best on Gram-positive bacteria, because their peptidoglycan is exposed. Gram-negative cells are partly protected by the outer membrane.
cards.searchQuery: lysozyme enzyme peptidoglycan tears saliva innate

cards.title: How does the normal microbiota protect against pathogens, and how can antibiotics undermine this?
cards.body:
It **competes** for nutrients and attachment sites, makes inhibitory products such as acids and bacteriocins, and stimulates the immune system.

Broad-spectrum antibiotics kill much of the flora, so resistant organisms can overgrow.

Example: after antibiotics, $\textit{Clostridioides difficile}$ can overgrow in the colon and cause colitis, and $\textit{Candida}$ can overgrow in the vagina.
cards.searchQuery: normal microbiota colonization resistance antibiotics Clostridioides difficile

cards.title: What are PAMPs and PRRs, and how do they start innate immune responses?
cards.body:
**PAMPs** (pathogen-associated molecular patterns) are conserved molecules found on microbes, and **PRRs** (pattern recognition receptors) are the host receptors that detect them.

PAMP-PRR binding triggers cytokine production, phagocyte activation and inflammation.

Example: LPS, flagellin, peptidoglycan and viral double-stranded RNA are PAMPs.
cards.searchQuery: PAMPs PRRs pattern recognition receptors innate immunity

cards.title: Which Toll-like receptor recognizes LPS from Gram-negative bacteria?
cards.body:
TLR4.

Binding of LPS (with the help of CD14 and MD-2) activates NF-$\kappa$B and the release of inflammatory cytokines. Excess release causes septic shock.
cards.searchQuery: TLR4 LPS recognition Toll-like receptor Gram-negative

cards.title: List the steps of phagocytosis in order.
cards.body:
1. **Chemotaxis** toward the microbe
2. **Adherence** (helped by opsonins)
3. **Ingestion** into a phagosome
4. **Fusion** with a lysosome to form a phagolysosome
5. **Digestion** by enzymes and reactive oxygen species
6. **Exocytosis** of the waste

Watch out: some pathogens avoid killing, such as $\textit{Mycobacterium tuberculosis}$, which blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion.
cards.searchQuery: phagocytosis steps chemotaxis adherence ingestion phagolysosome

cards.title: Which white blood cells, making up 50 to 70% of circulating leukocytes, are the first to arrive at a bacterial infection and form most of the pus?
cards.body:
Neutrophils.

They are short-lived phagocytes with multilobed nuclei. They kill microbes with enzymes, reactive oxygen species and neutrophil extracellular traps.

Key idea: high neutrophil counts (and "bands" from the bone marrow) suggest acute bacterial infection.
cards.searchQuery: neutrophils first responders bacterial infection pus

cards.title: How are monocytes related to macrophages, and what are their main functions in infection?
cards.body:
**Monocytes** circulate in blood and become **macrophages** when they enter tissues.

Macrophages phagocytose microbes and debris, secrete cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-$\alpha$, and present antigen to T cells.

Example: Kupffer cells (liver) and alveolar macrophages (lung) are tissue macrophages.
cards.searchQuery: monocytes macrophages differentiation phagocytosis antigen presentation

cards.title: Which cells, with long branching projections in the skin and mucosa, are the most effective antigen-presenting cells for activating naive T cells?
cards.body:
Dendritic cells.

They capture antigen, mature and migrate to lymph nodes, and present peptide on MHC molecules with costimulatory signals. They form the main link between innate and adaptive immunity.
cards.searchQuery: dendritic cells antigen presentation naive T cells lymph node

cards.title: How do natural killer (NK) cells recognize and kill virus-infected and tumor cells?
cards.body:
They kill cells that show **reduced MHC I** ("missing self"), and also cells coated by IgG through **ADCC**.

Killing uses perforin to make pores and granzymes to trigger apoptosis.

Why: many viruses and tumors down-regulate MHC I to hide from cytotoxic T cells, which makes them targets for NK cells instead.
cards.searchQuery: NK cells missing self MHC I perforin granzyme ADCC

cards.title: Which granulocytes defend against multicellular parasites such as helminths, and are often increased in allergy?
cards.body:
Eosinophils.

They release toxic granule proteins onto parasites that are too large to phagocytose, often when the parasite is coated with IgE.

Tip: a high eosinophil count suggests worm infection or allergic disease.
cards.searchQuery: eosinophils helminth parasites allergy IgE

cards.title: Which preformed mediator in mast cell granules causes vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and itching?
cards.body:
Histamine.

Mast cells release it in minutes after tissue damage or IgE-triggered activation. Increased vascular permeability lets fluid, complement and antibodies reach the tissue.

Example: antihistamines block H1 receptors to relieve allergic symptoms.
cards.searchQuery: histamine mast cells vasodilation vascular permeability

cards.title: What are the five cardinal signs of acute inflammation, with their Latin names?
cards.body:
**Redness** (rubor), **heat** (calor), **swelling** (tumor), **pain** (dolor) and **loss of function** (functio laesa).

Vasodilation causes redness and heat. Increased permeability causes swelling. Mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins cause pain.
cards.searchQuery: five cardinal signs inflammation rubor calor tumor dolor

cards.title: Which cytokines act as endogenous pyrogens, and how do they raise body temperature?
cards.body:
**IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-$\alpha$** act on the hypothalamus, where they induce prostaglandin E$_2$ and raise the temperature set point.

Moderate fever can slow bacterial growth, speed up immune cell activity and reduce iron available to microbes.

Watch out: exogenous pyrogens, such as LPS, trigger release of the endogenous ones.
cards.searchQuery: endogenous pyrogens IL-1 IL-6 TNF fever hypothalamus prostaglandin

cards.title: Which cytokines released by virus-infected cells make neighboring cells enter an antiviral state?
cards.body:
Interferons (type I: IFN-$\alpha$ and IFN-$\beta$).

Viral double-stranded RNA triggers their production. They induce proteins that degrade viral RNA and block translation in nearby cells, and they enhance NK cell activity.

Key idea: interferons do not save the infected cell; they protect its neighbors.
cards.searchQuery: type I interferon antiviral state alpha beta

cards.title: What are the three pathways of complement activation, and what triggers each?
cards.body:
**Classical**: antibody-antigen complexes bound by C1q. **Alternative**: spontaneous C3 hydrolysis on microbial surfaces. **Lectin**: mannose-binding lectin on microbial mannose.

All three converge on a **C3 convertase** that cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b.

Key idea: the classical pathway links adaptive immunity (antibody) to complement.
cards.searchQuery: complement pathways classical alternative lectin C3 convertase

cards.title: What are the three main outcomes of complement activation, and which fragments mediate them?
cards.body:
1. **Opsonization**: C3b coats microbes
2. **Inflammation**: C3a and C5a (anaphylatoxins) recruit and activate phagocytes
3. **Lysis**: the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) forms pores

Watch out: the MAC works mainly on Gram-negative bacteria, since the thick peptidoglycan of Gram-positives blocks it.
cards.searchQuery: complement functions opsonization anaphylatoxins membrane attack complex

cards.title: Deficiencies of the terminal complement components (C5 to C9) lead to recurrent infections with which genus of Gram-negative diplococci?
cards.body:
$\textit{Neisseria}$.

The membrane attack complex is the main defense against $\textit{Neisseria meningitidis}$ and $\textit{N. gonorrhoeae}$, so patients lacking it get repeated meningococcal disease.
cards.searchQuery: terminal complement deficiency C5-C9 Neisseria infections

cards.title: What is the term for coating a microbe with C3b or IgG so phagocytes can ingest it more efficiently?
cards.body:
Opsonization.

Phagocytes have receptors for C3b and the Fc portion of IgG. The coating bridges the microbe and the phagocyte, which speeds up phagocytosis.

Why: encapsulated bacteria like $\textit{Streptococcus pneumoniae}$ resist phagocytosis until opsonized.
cards.searchQuery: opsonization C3b IgG Fc receptors phagocytosis

cards.title: Which acute-phase protein, made by the liver in response to IL-6 and binding to bacterial phosphocholine, is a common blood marker of inflammation?
cards.body:
C-reactive protein (CRP).

It acts as an opsonin and activates the classical complement pathway. Levels rise within hours of infection or tissue injury.
cards.searchQuery: C-reactive protein acute phase marker inflammation liver IL-6

cards.title: Describe the basic structure of an antibody (IgG) and the roles of its Fab and Fc regions.
cards.body:
Two identical **heavy chains** and two identical **light chains**, joined by disulfide bonds into a Y shape.

The two **Fab** arms (variable regions) bind antigen. The **Fc** stem sets the antibody class and mediates effector functions such as complement activation and binding to phagocyte receptors.

Key idea: antigen specificity lives in the variable regions; function lives in the constant Fc region.
cards.searchQuery: antibody structure heavy light chains Fab Fc variable region

cards.title: Which antibody class is the most abundant in serum and the only one that crosses the placenta to protect the newborn?
cards.body:
IgG.

It is made mainly in the secondary response. IgG opsonizes bacteria, neutralizes toxins and viruses, and activates complement.

Example: maternal IgG gives a baby passive immunity for the first months of life.
cards.searchQuery: IgG antibody most abundant crosses placenta passive immunity

cards.title: Which antibody class is the first made in a primary response, circulates as a pentamer, and is the most efficient at activating complement?
cards.body:
IgM.

Its ten antigen-binding sites give strong agglutination. IgM is also the main antibody made by newborns.

Tip: IgM against a pathogen suggests recent or current infection; IgG alone suggests past infection or immunization.
cards.searchQuery: IgM antibody pentamer first response complement activation

cards.title: Which antibody class, a dimer with a secretory component, is found in tears, saliva, mucus and breast milk?
cards.body:
IgA (secretory IgA).

It guards mucosal surfaces by blocking attachment of pathogens to epithelium. Breast milk IgA protects the infant gut.

Watch out: selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency, and it is often mild.
cards.searchQuery: secretory IgA mucosal immunity breast milk dimer

cards.title: Which antibody class binds to Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils, triggers allergic reactions, and helps defend against helminths?
cards.body:
IgE.

It is present in very low concentration in serum. When allergen cross-links IgE bound to mast cells, they degranulate and release histamine.

Example: IgE is behind hay fever, food allergy and anaphylaxis.
cards.searchQuery: IgE antibody allergy mast cells helminths

cards.title: What is immunoglobulin class switching, and what signals drive it?
cards.body:
A B cell changes the **constant region** of its heavy chain (for example, from IgM to IgG) while keeping the same **variable region**, so antigen specificity does not change.

It requires T cell help (CD40L on the T cell binding CD40 on the B cell) and cytokines, which decide the class.

Example: IL-4 promotes switching to IgE; IFN-$\gamma$ promotes IgG.
cards.searchQuery: immunoglobulin class switching CD40 cytokines heavy chain constant

cards.title: What is affinity maturation, and where does it occur?
cards.body:
Repeated **somatic hypermutation** of antibody variable genes, followed by selection of B cells whose antibodies bind antigen more tightly.

It takes place in **germinal centers** of lymph nodes and spleen with the help of T follicular helper cells.

Key idea: antibodies in the late response bind the antigen better than those in the early response.
cards.searchQuery: affinity maturation somatic hypermutation germinal center

cards.title: How does the secondary antibody response differ from the primary response?
cards.body:
The secondary response is **faster** (lag of days, not 1 to 2 weeks), **larger**, **longer-lasting**, and mostly **IgG** with higher affinity.

The primary response is slower and first makes IgM.

Why: memory B and T cells already exist, so no new clones need to be selected.

Key idea: this is the principle behind vaccine boosters.
cards.searchQuery: primary versus secondary antibody response memory IgM IgG

cards.title: List the main ways antibodies help eliminate pathogens.
cards.body:
- **Neutralization** of toxins and viruses by blocking binding
- **Opsonization** for phagocytosis
- **Complement activation** (classical pathway)
- **ADCC** (NK cells kill antibody-coated targets)
- **Agglutination** and precipitation

Watch out: antibodies do not kill microbes directly; they flag them for other mechanisms.
cards.searchQuery: antibody functions neutralization opsonization complement ADCC agglutination

cards.title: How does the immune system generate billions of different antibody and T cell receptor specificities from a limited number of genes?
cards.body:
By **V(D)J recombination**: random joining of V, D and J gene segments in developing lymphocytes, with extra variation from imprecise joining.

The recombinase proteins RAG1 and RAG2 do the cutting. Combining heavy and light chains adds more diversity.

Watch out: this is a somatic DNA rearrangement in lymphocytes, not inherited variation.
cards.searchQuery: V(D)J recombination RAG1 RAG2 antibody diversity

cards.title: What two signals activate a B cell to make antibody against a protein antigen, and what does it become?
cards.body:
Signal 1 is antigen binding to the **B cell receptor**. Signal 2 is **help from a helper T cell** (CD40L-CD40 plus cytokines) that recognizes the processed peptide on MHC II.

The activated B cell becomes an **antibody-secreting plasma cell** or a **memory B cell**.

Example: capsular polysaccharides can sometimes activate B cells without T cell help, but memory is poor.
cards.searchQuery: B cell activation helper T cell CD40L plasma cell memory

cards.title: Which long-lived lymphocytes, produced during a first exposure, allow a faster and stronger response on re-exposure to the same antigen?
cards.body:
Memory cells (memory B and T cells).

They persist for years and respond faster, at a lower threshold, than naive cells. They underlie immunological memory and the protection from vaccines.
cards.searchQuery: memory B cells memory T cells immunological memory vaccine

cards.title: In which organ do T cell precursors mature, undergoing positive and negative selection?
cards.body:
The thymus.

Positive selection keeps T cells that can recognize self MHC, and negative selection removes those that bind self antigens too strongly. B cells mature in the **bone marrow** instead.

Key idea: T = thymus, B = bone marrow (for mammals).
cards.searchQuery: thymus T cell maturation positive negative selection

cards.title: What are the main functions of the Th1, Th2 and Th17 subsets of CD4$^+$ helper T cells?
cards.body:
- **Th1** (IFN-$\gamma$): activate macrophages against intracellular microbes
- **Th2** (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13): help B cells, IgE, and eosinophils against helminths
- **Th17** (IL-17): recruit neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi

Helper T cells recognize peptide on **MHC II**.

Example: Th1 responses control $\textit{Mycobacterium tuberculosis}$ by activating macrophages.
cards.searchQuery: Th1 Th2 Th17 helper T cell subsets functions cytokines

cards.title: Which T cells recognize viral peptides on MHC I and kill infected cells with perforin and granzymes?
cards.body:
Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), also called CD8$^+$ T cells.

Perforin forms pores in the target and granzymes enter and trigger apoptosis. CTLs also use the Fas-FasL pathway.

Key idea: CTLs kill infected cells, not free virus.
cards.searchQuery: cytotoxic T lymphocytes CD8 perforin granzyme MHC I

cards.title: Which CD4$^+$ T cells, marked by the transcription factor FOXP3, suppress immune responses and maintain self-tolerance?
cards.body:
Regulatory T cells (Tregs).

They secrete inhibitory cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-$\beta$. Loss of FOXP3 function causes severe autoimmunity (IPEX syndrome).
cards.searchQuery: regulatory T cells FOXP3 tolerance Treg IL-10

cards.title: What is costimulation, and what happens to a T cell that receives only the antigen signal?
cards.body:
Full T cell activation needs **signal 1** (TCR binds peptide-MHC) and **signal 2** (CD28 on the T cell binds B7 on the antigen-presenting cell).

Without signal 2, the T cell becomes **anergic** (unresponsive), which helps prevent reactions to self antigens.

Example: dendritic cells express B7 only after PAMP recognition, tying activation to danger.
cards.searchQuery: T cell costimulation CD28 B7 anergy signal 2

cards.title: How does antigen recognition by T cell receptors differ from that by B cell receptors?
cards.body:
The **TCR** recognizes only **peptide displayed on an MHC molecule**. The **BCR** (and secreted antibody) binds native antigen directly, including proteins, polysaccharides and lipids.

TCRs are never secreted, but antibodies are the secreted form of BCRs.

Watch out: T cells cannot see free, unprocessed antigen.
cards.searchQuery: T cell receptor versus B cell receptor antigen recognition MHC peptide

cards.title: What does the clonal selection theory state?
cards.body:
Each lymphocyte carries receptors of **one specificity**, made before any antigen exposure. An antigen **selects** the matching cells, which proliferate into a clone of effector and memory cells.

Self-reactive clones are removed or silenced during development.

Key idea: the antigen selects; it does not instruct the cell.
cards.searchQuery: clonal selection theory lymphocytes specificity expansion

cards.title: Which MHC class is found on all nucleated cells, presents peptides from inside the cell, and is recognized by CD8$^+$ T cells?
cards.body:
MHC class I.

It presents peptides made by proteasomal breakdown of cytosolic proteins, such as viral proteins in an infected cell. Cells loaded with foreign peptides are killed by CTLs.

Watch out: red blood cells lack nuclei and MHC I; so they are not targets of CTLs.
cards.searchQuery: MHC class I nucleated cells CD8 endogenous antigen presentation

cards.title: Which MHC class is found mainly on antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, and is recognized by CD4$^+$ T cells?
cards.body:
MHC class II.

It presents peptides from **extracellular** antigens that the cell has taken up and degraded in a phagolysosome. Recognition by a helper T cell then drives macrophage or B cell activation.

Mnemonic: "Rule of 8": CD4 $\times$ MHC II = 8, and CD8 $\times$ MHC I = 8.
cards.searchQuery: MHC class II antigen presenting cells CD4 exogenous antigen

cards.title: On which human chromosome are the genes of the major histocompatibility complex (HLA) located? Give the number only.
cards.body:
6

HLA genes are the most polymorphic in the human genome. They are inherited as a haplotype from each parent and expressed codominantly.

Example: siblings have a 25% chance of being a full HLA match.
cards.searchQuery: HLA genes chromosome 6 major histocompatibility complex

cards.title: How do the endogenous (MHC I) and exogenous (MHC II) antigen processing pathways differ?
cards.body:
**MHC I**: cytosolic proteins are cut by the proteasome, imported into the ER by TAP, and loaded onto MHC I. **MHC II**: antigens taken up by endocytosis are broken down in a phagolysosome and loaded onto MHC II, whose groove is protected by the invariant chain until then.

Key idea: where the antigen was made decides which MHC presents it.
cards.searchQuery: MHC I versus MHC II antigen processing proteasome TAP invariant chain

cards.title: Why do HLA mismatches cause graft rejection, and how are recipients protected?
cards.body:
The recipient's T cells recognize **foreign MHC molecules** on donor cells as non-self, and attack the graft.

Tissue typing aims to match HLA genes, and recipients receive **immunosuppressants** such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus, which block T cell activation.

Watch out: in graft-versus-host disease, the donor's T cells attack the recipient's tissues.
cards.searchQuery: transplant rejection HLA mismatch T cells immunosuppression

cards.title: How do superantigens such as toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) cause disease?
cards.body:
They bind **outside the peptide groove**, cross-linking MHC II on antigen-presenting cells with the T cell receptor V$\beta$ region.

This activates a large fraction of all T cells, causing massive release of cytokines (IL-2, IFN-$\gamma$, TNF-$\alpha$) and shock.

Example: $\textit{Staphylococcus aureus}$ makes TSST-1, and $\textit{Streptococcus pyogenes}$ makes pyrogenic exotoxins.
cards.searchQuery: superantigen TSST-1 cytokine storm toxic shock T cell Vbeta

cards.title: How do active and passive immunity differ, and what is an example of each?
cards.body:
**Active**: the person's own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells, as after infection or vaccination. It is slow to start but long-lasting. **Passive**: antibodies made elsewhere are transferred. It acts immediately but fades within weeks to months.

Example: passive immunity is seen in maternal IgG across the placenta, or in antitoxin given for botulism.
cards.searchQuery: active versus passive immunity natural artificial examples

cards.title: What are the advantages and risks of live attenuated vaccines?
cards.body:
They give **strong, long-lasting** immunity, often after one or two doses, since the weakened organism replicates and engages both antibody and T cell responses.

They can cause disease in immunocompromised people and are avoided in pregnancy.

Example: MMR, varicella and yellow fever vaccines are live attenuated.
cards.searchQuery: live attenuated vaccines advantages risks MMR contraindicated immunocompromised

cards.title: What is the term for a bacterial toxin that has been chemically inactivated but still induces protective antibodies, as in the tetanus vaccine?
cards.body:
A toxoid.

Vaccination with a toxoid triggers antibodies (antitoxin) that neutralize the real toxin. Diphtheria and tetanus vaccines both use toxoids, which is why disease is caused by toxin, not by the bacteria themselves.

Tip: because immunity wanes, tetanus boosters are given about every 10 years.
cards.searchQuery: toxoid vaccine tetanus diphtheria inactivated toxin

cards.title: Why are capsular polysaccharides linked to a protein carrier in conjugate vaccines such as Hib and pneumococcal vaccines?
cards.body:
Polysaccharides alone are **T-independent** antigens and give poor responses in infants, with little memory.

Linking them to a protein recruits **helper T cells**, which gives class switching, high-affinity IgG and memory.

Example: the Hib conjugate vaccine sharply reduced $\textit{Haemophilus influenzae}$ type b meningitis in children.
cards.searchQuery: conjugate vaccine polysaccharide protein carrier T-dependent Hib

cards.title: How does an mRNA vaccine produce immunity?
cards.body:
mRNA encoding an antigen (such as the viral spike protein) is delivered in **lipid nanoparticles**. Host cells **translate** it in the cytoplasm and display the protein, which triggers antibody and T cell responses.

The mRNA is degraded within days. It does not enter the nucleus or integrate into host DNA.

Watch out: it is not a live virus and cannot cause the infection.
cards.searchQuery: mRNA vaccine mechanism lipid nanoparticle spike protein translation

cards.title: For a disease with $R_0 = 4$, what percent of the population must be immune for herd immunity? Use $1 - 1/R_0$. Give the number only.
cards.body:
75

The threshold is $1 - \dfrac{1}{R_0} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.75$, or 75%.

Why: when enough people are immune, each case infects fewer than one new person on average, so the outbreak dies out.

Example: highly contagious measles ($R_0$ about 12 to 18) needs a coverage above about 92 to 95%.
cards.searchQuery: herd immunity threshold formula R0 1 - 1/R0

cards.title: What name is given to a substance, such as aluminum salts, added to a vaccine to boost the immune response to the antigen?
cards.body:
An adjuvant.

Adjuvants activate innate immune cells and prolong antigen exposure, so inactivated and subunit vaccines work better.

Example: alum is in hepatitis B and tetanus vaccines.
cards.searchQuery: vaccine adjuvant alum boosts immune response

cards.title: What is type I hypersensitivity, and what are two examples?
cards.body:
An **immediate** reaction in which allergen cross-links **IgE** on mast cells, causing release of histamine and other mediators within minutes.

Examples: hay fever, food allergy, asthma and **anaphylaxis**.

Key idea: it requires prior sensitization, when IgE was first made on an earlier exposure.
cards.searchQuery: type I hypersensitivity IgE mast cell degranulation anaphylaxis

cards.title: What is the first-line drug for treating anaphylaxis?
cards.body:
Epinephrine.

It raises blood pressure, relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and reduces swelling. It is given intramuscularly in the thigh, right away.

Watch out: antihistamines and steroids are only add-ons and do not replace epinephrine.
cards.searchQuery: anaphylaxis first-line treatment epinephrine intramuscular

cards.title: What is type II hypersensitivity, and what are two examples?
cards.body:
Antibodies (IgG or IgM) bind to antigens **on cell surfaces or tissue**, causing destruction by complement, phagocytes or ADCC.

Examples: ABO-incompatible transfusion reaction, hemolytic disease of the newborn, and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

Key idea: antibody plus a cell-bound target.
cards.searchQuery: type II hypersensitivity antibody cell surface transfusion reaction

cards.title: What is type III hypersensitivity, and what are two examples?
cards.body:
**Immune complexes** (antigen bound to antibody) deposit in tissues such as kidney, joints and vessels, activate complement and cause inflammation.

Examples: serum sickness, systemic lupus erythematosus and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Key idea: soluble antigen plus antibody, not cell-bound.
cards.searchQuery: type III hypersensitivity immune complex serum sickness lupus

cards.title: Which type of hypersensitivity is T cell-mediated, takes 48 to 72 hours to appear, and does not involve antibody?
cards.body:
Type IV (delayed-type hypersensitivity).

Sensitized T cells release cytokines that activate macrophages, causing induration and tissue damage.

Example: the tuberculin skin test and poison ivy contact dermatitis.
cards.searchQuery: type IV hypersensitivity delayed T cell tuberculin contact dermatitis

cards.title: How does an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus cause hemolytic disease of the newborn, and how is it prevented?
cards.body:
At delivery, fetal Rh$^+$ cells enter the mother's blood and sensitize her to make **anti-D IgG**. In a later Rh$^+$ pregnancy, this IgG **crosses the placenta** and destroys fetal red cells.

Prevention is **Rh immune globulin** (RhoGAM) given to the mother during pregnancy and after delivery. It clears fetal cells before she is sensitized.

Watch out: the first Rh$^+$ child is usually spared.
cards.searchQuery: Rh hemolytic disease newborn anti-D RhoGAM prevention

cards.title: Autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction cause which autoimmune disease with fatigable muscle weakness?
cards.body:
Myasthenia gravis.

The antibodies block or destroy the receptors, so nerve signals fail to trigger muscle contraction. It is a type II hypersensitivity, and thymus abnormalities are common.

Example: drooping eyelids and double vision are common first signs.
cards.searchQuery: myasthenia gravis acetylcholine receptor antibodies autoimmune

cards.title: How does untreated $\textit{Streptococcus pyogenes}$ pharyngitis lead to rheumatic fever?
cards.body:
By **molecular mimicry**: antibodies and T cells against the bacterial M protein cross-react with host proteins in the heart, joints and brain.

This can cause carditis and valve damage, arthritis and chorea. Prompt antibiotic treatment of strep throat prevents it.

Watch out: rheumatic fever is an immune reaction after the infection, not a direct bacterial invasion of the heart.
cards.searchQuery: rheumatic fever molecular mimicry Streptococcus pyogenes M protein

cards.title: What is severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), and why must live vaccines be avoided in affected infants?
cards.body:
A group of inherited disorders with **defective T cells and B cells** (and often NK cells), so there is no effective adaptive immunity.

Infants have severe, recurrent infections and need a stem cell transplant. A live vaccine strain can cause fatal disease because they cannot control it.

Example: X-linked SCID, from mutations in the common gamma chain of cytokine receptors.
cards.searchQuery: severe combined immunodeficiency SCID T B cells live vaccines

cards.title: How do endemic, epidemic and pandemic differ?
cards.body:
**Endemic**: a disease that is constantly present at a baseline level in a region. **Epidemic**: a sudden rise above the expected number of cases in a region. **Pandemic**: an epidemic that spreads across several countries or continents.

Example: malaria is endemic in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, while influenza can cause a pandemic.
cards.searchQuery: endemic epidemic pandemic definitions epidemiology

cards.title: How do incidence and prevalence differ in epidemiology?
cards.body:
**Incidence** is the number of **new** cases in a population over a period of time. **Prevalence** is the number of **existing** cases (new and old) at a point in time or over a period.

Why: a chronic disease with long survival, such as HIV on treatment, can have low incidence but high prevalence.
cards.searchQuery: incidence versus prevalence epidemiology new cases existing cases

cards.title: What is the term for the habitat or source in which a pathogen normally lives and multiplies, such as humans, animals or soil?
cards.body:
A reservoir.

It can be human (as with measles), animal or environmental. A reservoir differs from a **vector**, which only carries the organism to a new host.

Example: soil is the reservoir for $\textit{Clostridium tetani}$ spores, and rodents are the reservoir of $\textit{Yersinia pestis}$.
cards.searchQuery: reservoir of infection definition pathogen source

cards.title: What is the difference between a mechanical and a biological vector?
cards.body:
A **mechanical** vector carries the pathogen passively on its body, with no replication, as a fly carries bacteria from feces to food. In a **biological** vector, the pathogen **multiplies or develops**, and transmission is often by bite.

Example: $\textit{Anopheles}$ mosquitoes are biological vectors in which malaria parasites mature.
cards.searchQuery: mechanical vector versus biological vector disease transmission

cards.title: What is the term for an inanimate object, such as a doorknob or towel, that can carry and transmit pathogens?
cards.body:
A fomite.

Example: contaminated bed linens and medical equipment can spread MRSA or norovirus.

Tip: hand hygiene and surface disinfection break the fomite route.
cards.searchQuery: fomite definition inanimate object disease transmission

cards.title: What is the term for an infectious disease that is transmitted from animals to humans, such as rabies or brucellosis?
cards.body:
A zoonosis.

Transmission can be by bite, by contact with animal products, through contaminated food, or by vectors.

Example: $\textit{Toxoplasma gondii}$ (cats), $\textit{Salmonella}$ (poultry) and $\textit{Yersinia pestis}$ (rodent fleas) are zoonotic.
cards.searchQuery: zoonosis definition animal to human infectious disease

cards.title: What is an asymptomatic carrier, and why was "Typhoid Mary" an important example?
cards.body:
A carrier harbors and sheds a pathogen but shows **no symptoms**, so can spread it unknowingly.

Mary Mallon, a cook, carried $\textit{Salmonella}$ Typhi (in her gallbladder) and infected many people.

Key idea: chronic typhoid carriers often harbor the bacteria in the gallbladder.
cards.searchQuery: asymptomatic carrier Typhoid Mary Salmonella Typhi gallbladder

cards.title: State Koch's four postulates for establishing that a specific microbe causes a disease.
cards.body:
1. The microbe is **found in every case** of the disease and not in healthy hosts.
2. It is **isolated and grown** in pure culture.
3. The pure culture **causes the disease** when given to a healthy susceptible host.
4. The same microbe is **re-isolated** from the experimentally infected host.

Watch out: they fail for pathogens that cannot be cultured, for asymptomatic carriers, and for viruses without suitable hosts.
cards.searchQuery: Koch's postulates four steps causative agent limitations

cards.title: What does the basic reproduction number $R_0$ measure, and what value separates a spreading outbreak from one that dies out?
cards.body:
$R_0$ is the **average number of new infections** caused by one infected person in a fully susceptible population.

If $R_0 > 1$ the outbreak grows; if $R_0 < 1$ it declines.

Watch out: $R_0$ depends on the population and its behavior, not only on the pathogen.
cards.searchQuery: basic reproduction number R0 definition threshold 1

cards.title: In an outbreak, 20 of 400 diagnosed cases die. What is the case fatality rate, in percent? Give the number only.
cards.body:
5

Case fatality rate $= \dfrac{\text{deaths among cases}}{\text{number of cases}} \times 100 = \dfrac{20}{400} \times 100 = 5\%$.

Watch out: this is not the mortality rate, whose denominator is the whole population.
cards.searchQuery: case fatality rate calculation formula deaths cases

cards.title: What are healthcare-associated (nosocomial) infections, and what are two common examples?
cards.body:
Infections acquired **during medical care** that were not present or incubating on admission.

Examples: catheter-associated urinary tract infections, surgical site infections, ventilator-associated pneumonia, MRSA and $\textit{Clostridioides difficile}$ infections.

Tip: hand hygiene is the single most effective prevention measure.
cards.searchQuery: healthcare-associated infections nosocomial examples catheter MRSA

cards.title: What are the key features of $\textit{Staphylococcus aureus}$, and what does protein A do?
cards.body:
Gram-positive cocci in **clusters**, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive. It causes skin abscesses, food poisoning, toxic shock and endocarditis.

**Protein A** binds the **Fc region of IgG**, blocking opsonization and phagocytosis.

Example: preformed enterotoxin in food causes vomiting within hours.
cards.searchQuery: Staphylococcus aureus protein A Fc IgG virulence factors

cards.title: Which Lancefield group A, beta-hemolytic coccus causes strep throat and can lead to rheumatic fever?
cards.body:
$\textit{Streptococcus pyogenes}$.

Its M protein resists phagocytosis. It is bacitracin-sensitive and catalase-negative, and it also causes impetigo, scarlet fever and necrotizing fasciitis.

Example: sore throat with exudate, fever and no cough suggests strep.
cards.searchQuery: Streptococcus pyogenes group A strep throat M protein rheumatic fever

cards.title: Which encapsulated, alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive, lancet-shaped diplococcus is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia?
cards.body:
$\textit{Streptococcus pneumoniae}$.

Its polysaccharide capsule is the main virulence factor. It also causes otitis media, sinusitis and meningitis. It is bile-soluble.

Tip: optochin sensitivity separates it from other alpha-hemolytic streptococci.
cards.searchQuery: Streptococcus pneumoniae optochin alpha-hemolytic pneumonia capsule

cards.title: Which Gram-negative diplococcus causes meningitis with a petechial rash, and what is given as prophylaxis to close contacts?
cards.body:
$\textit{Neisseria meningitidis}$, with prophylaxis by **rifampin** (or ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone).

It colonizes the nasopharynx and spreads by respiratory droplets, with outbreaks in dormitories and barracks. Its LPS causes shock in meningococcemia.

Tip: vaccines cover serogroups A, C, W, Y and B.
cards.searchQuery: Neisseria meningitidis meningitis petechial rash rifampin prophylaxis

cards.title: How does $\textit{Neisseria gonorrhoeae}$ look on a Gram stain of urethral discharge, and why is there no effective vaccine?
cards.body:
**Gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils.**

It escapes immunity by constantly varying its pilin and Opa surface proteins (**antigenic variation**), so immune memory does not protect against reinfection.

Watch out: infection in women is often asymptomatic, and it can spread to cause pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility.
cards.searchQuery: Neisseria gonorrhoeae Gram-negative diplococci neutrophils antigenic variation

cards.title: Which acid-fast bacillus causes tuberculosis, with caseating granulomas in the lung?
cards.body:
$\textit{Mycobacterium tuberculosis}$.

It survives inside macrophages. A Th1 response with IFN-$\gamma$ activates macrophages and builds granulomas that wall off the bacteria. Latent infection can reactivate years later.

Example: a positive tuberculin skin test reflects type IV hypersensitivity.
cards.searchQuery: Mycobacterium tuberculosis acid-fast caseating granuloma macrophages

cards.title: Which spore-forming, toxin-producing anaerobe causes antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis?
cards.body:
$\textit{Clostridioides difficile}$.

Antibiotics wipe out competing gut flora, so the spores germinate and make toxins A and B. Alcohol hand rubs do not kill spores, so soap and water handwashing is needed.

Example: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin treats it.
cards.searchQuery: Clostridioides difficile antibiotic-associated colitis toxins A B spores

cards.title: Which Gram-negative rod, using P fimbriae to attach to the urinary tract, causes most uncomplicated urinary tract infections?
cards.body:
$\textit{Escherichia coli}$ (uropathogenic strains).

It ascends from the urethra to the bladder and sometimes the kidney. Women are affected more often because the urethra is shorter.

Tip: lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar (pink) with a positive indole test suggest $\textit{E. coli}$.
cards.searchQuery: Escherichia coli urinary tract infection uropathogenic P fimbriae

cards.title: How does enterohemorrhagic $\textit{E. coli}$ O157:H7 cause hemolytic uremic syndrome?
cards.body:
It makes **Shiga-like toxin**, which inhibits the 60S ribosomal subunit and causes bloody diarrhea.

The toxin damages endothelial cells of small vessels, producing hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and kidney failure.

Watch out: antibiotics are generally avoided because they may increase toxin release.
cards.searchQuery: EHEC O157:H7 Shiga toxin hemolytic uremic syndrome

cards.title: What are the key features of typhoid fever and its cause, $\textit{Salmonella}$ Typhi?
cards.body:
A Gram-negative rod, non-lactose fermenter, with a **Vi capsule**, spread by the **fecal-oral** route with humans as the only reservoir.

It invades the intestine and multiplies inside macrophages. Sustained fever, rose-colored spots on the abdomen and bowel perforation can follow.

Example: unlike nontyphoidal $\textit{Salmonella}$, which is a zoonosis from poultry and eggs.
cards.searchQuery: Salmonella Typhi typhoid fever Vi capsule fecal-oral rose spots

cards.title: How does cholera toxin cause the profuse watery diarrhea of cholera?
cards.body:
It **ADP-ribosylates the G$_s$ protein**, which keeps adenylate cyclase on. The rise in cAMP makes the intestinal cells pump out $\ce{Cl-}$ and water.

Result: "rice-water" stool and rapid dehydration. The key treatment is oral or intravenous rehydration.

Key idea: $\textit{Vibrio cholerae}$ is a comma-shaped Gram-negative rod that stays in the gut lumen and does not invade.
cards.searchQuery: cholera toxin ADP-ribosylation Gs cAMP rice-water diarrhea

cards.title: Which enzyme lets $\textit{Helicobacter pylori}$ survive stomach acid by making ammonia?
cards.body:
Urease.

It splits urea into $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{NH3}$, which neutralizes acid around the bacterium. $\textit{H. pylori}$ is linked to gastritis, peptic ulcers and gastric cancer, and the urea breath test detects it.
cards.searchQuery: Helicobacter pylori urease ammonia stomach acid ulcer

cards.title: Which spirochete, too thin to be seen on a Gram stain and visualized by dark-field microscopy, causes syphilis?
cards.body:
$\textit{Treponema pallidum}$.

The primary stage causes a painless chancre; the secondary stage causes a rash, including on the palms and soles. It crosses the placenta (congenital syphilis). Penicillin G is the treatment.

Watch out: it cannot be grown on routine artificial media.
cards.searchQuery: Treponema pallidum syphilis spirochete dark-field chancre

cards.title: Which spirochete causes Lyme disease, and which tick transmits it?
cards.body:
$\textit{Borrelia burgdorferi}$, transmitted by $\textit{Ixodes}$ (deer) ticks.

The early sign is an expanding rash, erythema migrans. Later stages can involve joints, heart and nerves. The tick usually needs to feed for more than 24 to 36 hours to transmit it.

Tip: doxycycline is the usual treatment.
cards.searchQuery: Borrelia burgdorferi Lyme disease Ixodes tick erythema migrans

cards.title: $\textit{Chlamydia trachomatis}$ is an obligate intracellular bacterium. Which of its two forms is the infectious, metabolically inactive one?
cards.body:
The elementary body.

It enters the host cell and turns into a **reticulate body**, which replicates by binary fission inside an inclusion. The reticulate bodies then change back into elementary bodies that are released.

Example: $\textit{C. trachomatis}$ is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection and the cause of trachoma.
cards.searchQuery: Chlamydia trachomatis elementary body reticulate body life cycle

cards.title: Which Gram-negative bacterium, spread by aerosols from contaminated water systems and cooling towers, causes Legionnaires' disease?
cards.body:
$\textit{Legionella pneumophila}$.

It is a facultative intracellular pathogen of macrophages and amoebae. It does not spread person to person, and it needs buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar to grow.

Example: outbreaks are linked to hotels, hospitals and air-conditioning systems.
cards.searchQuery: Legionella pneumophila Legionnaires disease water aerosol BCYE agar

cards.title: How do tetanus toxin and botulinum toxin differ in their effects on nerve signaling and the type of paralysis?
cards.body:
**Tetanus toxin** blocks release of the inhibitory transmitters GABA and glycine, causing **spastic** paralysis. **Botulinum toxin** blocks release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing **flaccid** paralysis.

Both cleave SNARE proteins, but at different neurons.

Example: tetanus gives lockjaw and spasms; botulism gives drooping eyelids, then descending weakness.
cards.searchQuery: tetanus toxin versus botulinum toxin spastic flaccid paralysis SNARE

cards.title: How does $\textit{Bordetella pertussis}$ cause whooping cough?
cards.body:
It colonizes the **ciliated respiratory epithelium** and makes toxins (including **pertussis toxin**) that paralyze cilia and impair host defenses.

The disease passes through catarrhal, paroxysmal (whooping cough) and convalescent stages. Immunity wanes, so boosters are given in adolescents and adults, and in pregnancy.

Watch out: infants are at the highest risk of severe disease.
cards.searchQuery: Bordetella pertussis whooping cough pertussis toxin cilia

cards.title: What is the molecular action of diphtheria toxin, and what does it cause in the throat?
cards.body:
It **ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 (EF-2)**, which blocks protein synthesis and kills host cells.

The dead cells, fibrin and bacteria form a gray **pseudomembrane** in the throat that can obstruct the airway. The toxin gene is carried by a prophage.

Example: the DTaP vaccine uses diphtheria toxoid.
cards.searchQuery: diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylation EF-2 pseudomembrane Corynebacterium

cards.title: Which obligate intracellular bacterium causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and how does the rash typically spread?
cards.body:
$\textit{Rickettsia rickettsii}$, spread by ticks (such as $\textit{Dermacentor}$).

The rash begins on the **wrists and ankles** and spreads **centrally** to the trunk, often involving palms and soles. Doxycycline should be given early.

Watch out: it can be fatal if untreated, and the rash may be absent early.
cards.searchQuery: Rickettsia rickettsii Rocky Mountain spotted fever tick rash wrists ankles

cards.title: What are the key features of hepatitis B virus (HBV), and what does the surface antigen (HBsAg) indicate?
cards.body:
A partially double-stranded **DNA** virus that replicates through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase. It spreads by blood and sexual contact and from mother to baby.

**HBsAg** in blood means current infection. **Anti-HBs** alone indicates vaccine-induced immunity or past recovery.

Key idea: chronic infection raises the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer.
cards.searchQuery: hepatitis B virus HBsAg anti-HBs DNA reverse transcriptase chronic infection

cards.title: What is the post-exposure prophylaxis for a person bitten by a possibly rabid animal?
cards.body:
**Wash the wound** thoroughly, then give **rabies immune globulin** (infiltrated around the wound) plus a **rabies vaccine** series.

The virus travels along peripheral nerves to the brain, with an incubation period of weeks to months. Once symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal.

Key idea: this is passive plus active immunization, started before the virus reaches the nervous system.
cards.searchQuery: rabies post-exposure prophylaxis immune globulin vaccine wound washing

cards.title: Which encapsulated yeast, found in pigeon droppings and seen with India ink, is a major cause of meningitis in AIDS patients?
cards.body:
$\textit{Cryptococcus neoformans}$.

Inhalation leads to lung infection, and in people with poor T cell immunity it spreads to the meninges. The capsule appears as a clear halo around the yeast in India ink.

Tip: the cryptococcal antigen test of cerebrospinal fluid is sensitive for diagnosis.
cards.searchQuery: Cryptococcus neoformans India ink pigeon droppings meningitis AIDS

cards.title: Which fungus causes the opportunistic pneumonia that is a classic AIDS-defining illness when the CD4 count falls below about 200 cells per $\mu$L?
cards.body:
$\textit{Pneumocystis jirovecii}$.

Chest imaging shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is both the treatment and the prophylaxis for patients at risk.

Watch out: the organism infecting humans was formerly named $\textit{P. carinii}$.
cards.searchQuery: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia AIDS CD4 200 trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

cards.title: What are the small white spots on the buccal mucosa that appear before the rash of measles called?
cards.body:
Koplik spots.

Measles typically begins with fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis. The maculopapular rash starts on the face and spreads downward. The virus is highly contagious, and the MMR vaccine prevents it.
cards.searchQuery: Koplik spots measles buccal mucosa before rash

cards.title: Which herpesvirus infects B cells and causes infectious mononucleosis?
cards.body:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

Symptoms are fever, sore throat and swollen lymph nodes. Blood smears show **atypical lymphocytes**, which are mostly reactive CD8$^+$ T cells. The heterophile antibody (Monospot) test is often positive.

Watch out: EBV is also linked to Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
cards.searchQuery: Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis B cells atypical lymphocytes

cards.title: How do bacterial exotoxins and endotoxin differ in chemical nature, source and toxicity?
cards.body:
**Exotoxins** are secreted **proteins** (often from Gram-positive or Gram-negative cells), very potent and specific, and they can be converted to toxoids. **Endotoxin** is **LPS (lipid A)** of the Gram-negative outer membrane, released on cell lysis, with weaker, general effects such as fever and shock.

Exotoxins are generally heat-labile; endotoxin is heat-stable.

Example: botulinum toxin is an exotoxin; LPS in meningococcemia is the endotoxin.
cards.searchQuery: exotoxin versus endotoxin differences protein LPS toxoid

cards.title: What makes $\textit{Shigella}$ a cause of bloody dysentery even at a very low infectious dose?
cards.body:
It **invades colonic epithelial cells** and spreads cell to cell, and $\textit{Shigella dysenteriae}$ makes **Shiga toxin**.

A dose of only about 10 to 100 organisms can cause illness, so person-to-person spread by the fecal-oral route is easy. It is nonmotile and does not ferment lactose.

Watch out: stomach acid does not stop it, as it is relatively acid-resistant.
cards.searchQuery: Shigella dysentery low infectious dose Shiga toxin invasion
